items.title: The workshop
items.text: The workshop at the end of the lane was never locked. Anyone could walk in, take a chair from the corner, and watch the old carpenter work. He did not talk much while his hands were busy, but he did not mind an audience either. Most visitors expected him to move quickly, the way people move in films, with a flourish and a clean result in a single stroke. Instead he moved slowly, and he stopped often. He would lift a plane, sight along the board, set the plane down, and touch the wood with the flat of his palm as if he were checking a child for fever. Only then would he make the next pass. When someone finally asked why he paused so much, he laughed and said that speed was the last thing a hand learns. "First the hand learns where things are," he said. "Then it learns how hard to press. Then it learns when to stop. Speed comes on its own, a year later, when you have stopped asking for it." He held up a chisel with a handle worn pale where his thumb had rested for decades. "This did not happen in a week." His apprentices tended to fight that advice. They wanted to cut a joint in an afternoon and see it close without a gap. They pushed, the chisel wandered, and the joint came out loose. He never scolded them. He asked them to cut the same joint again the next morning, and the morning after that, and to write down what had gone wrong each time. After a month, the notebooks were more useful than the joints. They showed which mistakes repeated and which ones had quietly disappeared. There is a lesson in that for any skill that lives in the hands. The first attempts feel clumsy because the body has no map yet; every movement has to be planned, and planning is slow. Practice does not make the planning faster so much as it makes the planning unnecessary. The hand simply goes to the right place, and the mind is free to think about the next thing. You cannot rush that change, but you can make room for it: short sessions, honest notes, and a willingness to repeat the plain exercises that nobody wants to watch. On the wall above his bench he kept a single card with three words written in pencil: look, feel, again. Visitors assumed it was a motto. It was really a checklist, and he followed it every day.

items.title: River notes
items.text: The river changes its voice with the seasons. In early spring it is loud and brown, full of snowmelt from the hills, and it carries branches past the town faster than a person can walk. By midsummer it has dropped to a thin, clear murmur that slides over pale stones, and children wade across at the ford without getting their knees wet. In autumn the leaves arrive first, a slow parade of yellow and red, and then the rain returns and the water rises again. I began keeping notes on the river three years ago, mostly out of curiosity. Each morning I walked to the footbridge, looked at the painted gauge on the old pier, and wrote the level in a small green book. I added the weather, the color of the water, and anything unusual: a heron standing on one leg, a broken oar caught against the pier, a line of foam that meant the mill had opened its gates upstream. The notes were not scientific. They were simply regular, and regular notes turn out to be surprisingly powerful. After the first year I could see patterns that I had never noticed while living beside the water. The level rose about two days after heavy rain in the hills, not on the same day. A dry week in March lowered the river more than a dry week in June, because the ground was still cold and did not hold water in the same way. The heron came back to the same stone every morning in October, as if it had an appointment. None of this was hidden. I had just never looked at the river twice in the same way. That is the quiet value of a record. Memory is generous to good days and harsh to bad ones, so it tells a misleading story. A notebook does not care how you felt. It says that on Tuesday the level was 41 centimeters and the water was the color of tea, and it says the same thing a year later when you have forgotten Tuesday entirely. Put enough of those plain entries together and a shape appears, one that no single morning could have shown you. Some neighbors thought the habit was odd. Why stand on a bridge in the rain to write down a number? I understand the question, but I have stopped trying to answer it with words. Instead I show them the green books, open to any page, and let them read what the river was doing on their birthday.

items.title: Bread before dawn
items.text: The bakery on the corner begins its day at four in the morning, long before the street lamps switch off. The first person through the back door turns on the ovens, because they need an hour to reach full heat, and then fills the big kettle for tea. Nobody speaks until the tea is ready. After that the room fills with a steady, practiced noise: flour poured into steel bowls, the thump of dough turned out onto the table, the scrape of a bench knife cutting it into equal pieces. What surprises visitors is how little the bakers measure by eye. They weigh everything, even the water, and they write the weights on a board by the sink. The recipe for the country loaf has not changed in eleven years, but the dough is different every day. It depends on the temperature of the room, the humidity, the age of the flour, and the mood of the starter that lives in a covered jar on the top shelf. So the bakers adjust. On a cold morning they use warmer water; on a humid one they hold back a little of it. They make these changes calmly, because they have seen the same problems hundreds of times. Shaping is the part that takes the longest to learn. A new baker usually presses too hard, tearing the surface, or works too gently, leaving the loaf slack and flat. The experienced hands move in short, confident strokes that look almost careless. They fold the dough toward the body, turn it a quarter, fold again, and then drag it across the table so that the surface tightens into a smooth skin. Four seconds, maybe five. Asked how they know when a loaf is right, the bakers usually shrug and say that it simply feels right. What they mean is that they have shaped many thousands of loaves and have kept the ones that worked. By six o'clock the first trays come out of the ovens, and the smell reaches the street. The early customers are always the same: a nurse coming off the night shift, two builders on their way to a site, a man who walks his dog and buys one roll for himself and a smaller one for the dog. They do not see the four hours of work behind the counter. They see bread, warm and ordinary, which is exactly the point. Good practice disappears into the thing it makes.

items.title: The night bus
items.text: The last bus leaves the central station at twenty past midnight. It is never full, and it is never empty. There are always a few regular passengers who nod to the driver as they board and take the same seats every night: a cook still wearing checked trousers, a student with a heavy bag of books, an older woman who works at the hospital laundry and sleeps with her head against the window until her stop. Between them are the strangers, people who missed an earlier connection or stayed too long at a party and now sit very upright, watching the dark streets for a landmark they recognize. The driver has worked this route for nine years. She knows where the road is uneven and slows before the bump near the bakery without thinking about it. She knows which traffic lights change quickly and which ones hold her for a full minute on an empty street. She knows that the student will fall asleep and needs a gentle word at the university gate, and that the cook will want to get off one stop early to buy cigarettes. None of this is written in a manual. It is simply what happens when a person repeats the same journey, carefully, hundreds of times. On quiet nights she practices a small game. She tries to arrive at each stop exactly on the minute printed on the timetable, not early and not late. It is harder than it sounds. A single passenger fumbling for change can cost thirty seconds; a green wave of lights can gain a minute. She adjusts her speed in tiny steps, never rushing, and keeps a mental note of where she lost or gained time. When she gets it right from start to finish, she says nothing, but she smiles at the empty road for a moment before turning back toward the depot. Passengers rarely notice any of this. They notice when the bus is late, of course, and they notice a rough stop that sends a bag sliding across the floor. When the ride is smooth and the timing is exact, it feels like nothing at all, and they read their phones or close their eyes. That is fine with her. She has decided that the best version of her work is the one that nobody has to think about, and she is patient enough to keep chasing it, one quiet night at a time.

items.title: Lighthouse keeping
items.text: For most of its history the lighthouse on the northern point needed a keeper every night of the year. The lamp had to be lit at dusk, the lens had to be cleaned of salt and soot, and the clockwork that turned the light had to be wound every few hours so that the beam kept its steady rhythm across the water. Ships knew the lighthouse by that rhythm: two short flashes, a pause, and one long flash. If the pattern faltered, a captain miles offshore might mistake it for another light and set the wrong course. The keepers kept a log, and several of those logs survive in the small museum at the harbor. They are not dramatic documents. Most entries follow the same form: the time the lamp was lit, the weather, the state of the sea, the number of times the clockwork was wound, and the time the lamp was put out in the morning. Occasionally there is a note about a storm, a passing ship that signaled, or a gull that broke a pane of the lantern room. Page after page, the handwriting stays neat and the columns stay straight. What the logs show, above all, is a kind of patient attention. The keepers could not see the ships they were helping, and they rarely learned whether their light had mattered on any given night. Their work was judged by its consistency, not by its visible results. So they built habits that did not depend on mood. They climbed the same stairs at the same times, checked the same brass fittings in the same order, and wrote everything down, even when nothing had happened. A blank night was still recorded as a night. The lamp was automated long ago, and the last keeper left the point before I was born. Yet the building still carries traces of that daily routine. The stone steps are worn into shallow bowls where thousands of boots landed in the same place. The handrail is polished smooth at the height of a tired hand. It is easy to imagine someone climbing in the dark, counting the steps without looking, knowing by feel exactly where each one would be. That knowledge was not a talent. It was the slow deposit of repetition, laid down one night at a time, until the body could do the work while the mind watched the sea.

items.title: A small garden
items.text: My garden is not large. It is a narrow strip behind the house, about four meters wide and twelve meters long, with a fence on one side and a brick wall on the other. When we moved in, it held nothing but coarse grass, a rusted wheelbarrow, and a rose bush that had been left alone for so long that it had climbed halfway up the wall. I had no experience with plants, and I assumed that a garden was something you designed once and then enjoyed. I was wrong about that, and I am glad I was. The first season was mostly a list of mistakes. I planted tomatoes in the shade of the wall, where they grew tall and pale and produced three small fruits. I sowed lettuce too thickly and then felt too guilty to thin it, so the seedlings strangled one another. I watered in the heat of the afternoon, which wasted half the water and scorched the leaves. By August the garden looked tired and so did I. The only real success was the rose, which I had left alone, and which bloomed without any help from me. In the second year I started a notebook. Every weekend I wrote down what I had planted, where, and when, along with the weather and anything I noticed: which bed dried out first, where the slugs gathered, how many hours of sun reached each corner. It was dull work, and I often wanted to skip it. But by the end of that summer the notebook knew my garden better than I did. It showed that the far corner received six hours of direct sun while the corner by the house received barely two. It showed that the beans did well when I planted them a week later than the packet suggested. Now, in the fifth year, the garden mostly works. The tomatoes grow against the fence where the light is strong, the lettuce is sown in short rows every two weeks, and I water in the early morning before work. None of these changes were clever. They were small corrections, repeated and recorded, that added up over several seasons. People sometimes ask what my secret is, and I tell them the truth: I pay attention, I write it down, and I try again next year. That is less exciting than a secret, but it has the advantage of being true.

items.title: Reading old maps
items.text: Old maps are honest about what their makers did not know. On a chart drawn two centuries ago, the coastline near a busy port is traced in careful detail, every inlet and sandbar marked with soundings in tiny numbers. Farther along, where fewer ships had sailed, the line becomes smoother and more confident, which is a sign that it was guessed. Farther still, the coast simply stops, and the paper is left blank or filled with a note in faded ink: "Coast not surveyed." I have come to like those notes more than the decorated corners. A map is a record of attention. Wherever the surveyors spent time, the detail is rich: hills are shaded, streams are named, and the roads bend exactly where they bend on the ground. Wherever they hurried, the map is thin. You can read the history of the survey in the texture of the lines, the way you can read a person's habits in the wear on their shoes. The blank spaces are not failures. They are simply places where the work had not yet been done. There is a temptation, when copying an old map, to fill in the blanks. It feels untidy to leave a coast unfinished, and a confident line looks better on the wall. Some later mapmakers gave in to that temptation. They connected the known points with graceful curves, added a few invented islands, and sold the result as complete. Sailors who trusted those maps sometimes paid for it. A guess drawn with the same ink as a measurement is more dangerous than a blank, because it hides the difference between what is known and what is hoped. I think about this when I look at any kind of record, including my own. It is easy to round a number up, to remember a good week as typical, or to write down "about the same as usual" instead of checking. Each of those small choices smooths the line and hides a blank. A more useful habit is to mark the unknown plainly: not measured, not checked, not sure. It looks less impressive, but it tells the next reader, who is often your future self, exactly where the solid ground ends. The best maps in the museum are not the most beautiful ones. They are the ones where you can see the surveyors thinking: a hill drawn twice and corrected, a river marked "course uncertain," a depth given with a small question mark. They trusted their readers with the truth, and that is why they are still worth reading.

items.title: The slow train
items.text: There is a faster way to reach the coast, but I prefer the slow train. It leaves from the small platform at the edge of town, the one with a single bench and a timetable pinned behind cloudy plastic, and it stops at every village along the valley. The whole journey takes three hours and ten minutes. The express does it in ninety. Most people take the express, and I understand why, but they miss the part of the trip that I enjoy most, which is watching the landscape change one small step at a time. In the first hour the train follows the river through farmland. The fields are divided by low stone walls, and in spring the lambs run away from the noise and then stop, confused, as the carriages pass. In the second hour the valley narrows and the line climbs through a forest of dark pines. The air cools; you can feel it through the window. There is a tunnel, then another, and after the second tunnel the train comes out onto a ridge where the whole valley lies behind you, small and green. In the third hour the land drops toward the sea, the pines give way to gorse and heather, and the light becomes wider and paler until, just before the last station, you catch the first gray line of water between two hills. On the express, that sequence is compressed into a blur. You leave the town, you read for a while, and then you are at the coast. The destination is the same, but the journey has no shape. On the slow train, each change arrives separately, and there is time to notice it before the next one begins. I have made the trip perhaps forty times, and I still find something new: a heron in a ditch, a farmhouse with its shutters painted a different color, a path through the pines that I have never walked but have now memorized. I think skills are learned more like the slow train than the express. We would like to jump straight from the first awkward attempt to easy mastery, but the body does not work that way. It needs to pass through every village. Each stage has its own small lessons, and skipping them leaves gaps that show up later as hesitation or error. When I am impatient with slow progress, I remind myself of the ridge after the second tunnel, and how much better the view is when you have climbed to it one curve at a time.

items.title: Weather on the hill
items.text: The weather station on the hill above our village is nothing more than a white wooden box on four legs, a rain gauge, and a wind vane that squeaks when the wind swings to the north. A retired schoolteacher has read it every morning at nine o'clock for twenty-six years. She records the highest and lowest temperatures of the past day, the rainfall in millimeters, the direction of the wind, and a short description of the sky. She has missed only a handful of days, and on each of those days a neighbor read the instruments for her and wrote their initials beside the numbers. Her records have become quietly famous. Researchers from the university have visited twice to copy them, because a long, careful series from a single place is rare and valuable. The official stations nearby have moved, been rebuilt, or changed their instruments several times, which creates small jumps in their data that are hard to correct. The box on the hill has stayed exactly where it is, painted the same white every spring, read at the same hour by the same careful hand. Its numbers can be compared across decades without worrying that the method changed underneath them. She is proud of that consistency, but she is also strict about it. When the old thermometer cracked eight years ago, she did not simply replace it and carry on. She ran the new thermometer beside the old one's replacement for a full month, wrote both readings every morning, and made a note in the margin explaining the change. "If I don't say what changed," she told me, "then someone will think the hill got warmer overnight." That margin note is exactly the kind of detail that makes her records trustworthy. Visitors sometimes ask whether the work is boring. She admits that most days are ordinary; the sky is gray, the wind is from the west, and it rains a little. But she says the ordinary days are the whole point. Anyone can remember a great storm. Only a patient record can tell you that this March was drier than the last twenty, or that frosts now end nine days earlier than they did when she started. Those facts are built from ordinary mornings, written down without fuss, one after another, until the pattern is strong enough to speak for itself.

items.title: The library at closing
items.text: In the last half hour before the library closes, the building changes its mood. The afternoon crowd has gone home, the children's corner is empty, and the only sounds are the hum of the old heating pipes and the soft thud of returned books landing in the metal cart. A few readers remain at the long tables near the windows. They look up now and then at the clock above the desk, calculate how many pages they can still finish, and bend back over their work with renewed concentration. The librarian on the evening shift uses this time to reshelve. She pushes the cart slowly down the aisles and slides each book into its place with a small, precise movement of her wrist. She does not need to read the spine labels closely anymore. After eleven years she knows the shape of the collection the way a person knows the rooms of their own house in the dark: history is past the second pillar, poetry is on the low shelves under the stairs, and the large atlases lie flat on the bottom row because they are too heavy to stand. Reshelving is not glamorous work, but a library depends on it completely. A book in the wrong place is effectively lost. It might sit unnoticed for years, three shelves away from where the catalog says it should be, while readers search for it and give up. So the librarian checks her work. Every evening she chooses one shelf at random and reads it slowly from end to end, looking for anything out of order. Most nights she finds nothing. Now and then she finds a single book that someone has returned to the wrong gap, and she moves it back with quiet satisfaction. At ten minutes to closing she walks through the reading room and says, in a low voice, that the library will close soon. Nobody complains. The regular readers have learned to finish a chapter, mark their place, and pack up without being asked twice. At closing time she switches off the lights in sections, starting at the back, so that the room darkens gradually toward the door. Then she locks up, checks the handle twice, and walks home, leaving behind a building where every book, as far as she knows, is exactly where it belongs.

items.title: Repairing a bicycle
items.text: The bicycle had been leaning against the shed for four winters when I finally decided to repair it. The tires were flat and cracked, the chain was brown with rust, and the brake cables had seized inside their housings. My first instinct was to take it to a shop, but the repair shop in town had a waiting list of three weeks, and I was curious whether I could do the work myself. I borrowed a set of tools from a neighbor, found a manual in the library, and cleared a space on the garage floor. The manual was clear, but it assumed a kind of knowledge that I did not have. It said to "remove the rear wheel," as if that were a single action. In practice it involved shifting to the smallest gear, opening the brake, loosening two nuts that had not moved in a decade, and working the chain off the cog without dropping it into the dirt. The first time took me forty minutes and a fair amount of language that I will not repeat. The second time, a week later, took six minutes. Nothing about the bicycle had changed; my hands had simply learned the order of the steps. I made a habit of writing short notes as I worked. They were not elegant: "left brake nut is 10 mm, not 9," "chain tool pin goes in from the outside," "clean the rim before fitting new pads or they squeal." But each note saved me from repeating a mistake, and together they turned into a personal manual more useful than the printed one. When a friend asked me to look at her bicycle, I realized that I could explain each step without hesitation, because I had written down every place where I had once been confused. The finished bicycle is not beautiful. The paint is scratched, the saddle is mismatched, and one mudguard rattles on rough roads. But it runs smoothly, the brakes stop firmly, and the gears change with a crisp click. More importantly, I know how every part of it works. When something goes wrong, I no longer feel helpless. I turn the bicycle over, look carefully, and try the simplest fix first. Most problems, it turns out, are small ones that have been ignored for too long, and most repairs are just patience applied in the right order.

items.title: Letters from the coast
items.text: Every summer my grandfather wrote letters from the coast. He rented the same small cottage for three weeks each year, a stone building with a green door and a view of the harbor, and from there he sent long letters to everyone in the family. He wrote in pencil on lined paper, filling both sides of each sheet, and he always began the same way: "The tide is out, the gulls are loud, and I have nothing important to report." Then he reported everything. He described the fishing boats leaving before dawn and returning in the early afternoon, low in the water with their catch. He wrote about the woman who sold fruit from a cart by the church and never gave change in coins, only in extra plums. He noted the weather in careful detail, the way a sailor might: wind from the southwest, light rain until ten, clearing by noon, a sharp cold evening with stars. When I was young I skipped those parts and looked for the stories. Now I read the weather first, because it tells me exactly what kind of day he was living. After he died, my mother gathered the letters into a box, sorted by year. There are thirty-one summers in that box. Reading them in order is a strange and moving experience. At first nothing seems to change: the boats, the fruit cart, the green door. Then you notice small shifts. The fruit seller retires and her daughter takes over the cart. The fishing fleet shrinks from nine boats to five. His handwriting grows larger and less steady, and the letters become a little shorter each year, although they never stop describing the tide. I have started writing letters of my own, not from the coast but from ordinary weeks at home. I try to follow his method: begin with the plain facts, write down what I actually saw rather than what I expected to see, and do not worry about whether anything important happened. It is harder than it sounds. My first letters were full of opinions and empty of details. Slowly I am learning to look first and judge later, to notice the tide before I decide what it means. Perhaps in thirty years someone will read them in order and see the small changes that I am too close to notice now.

items.title: The fixed passage
items.text: Once a month, the same passage returns. It does not change, and that is the whole point of it. A new text would test how well you read something unfamiliar; this one tests how well each hand and each layout has kept what it learned. The words are ordinary on purpose: a kitchen table, a window, a kettle beginning to hum, a cat that has decided the warm spot by the radiator belongs to her. There are commas and full stops, a few capital letters, a question or two, and the occasional number, such as the 7 steps up to the front door or the 12 jars of jam lined up on the shelf. Nothing here should surprise you after the first reading, and so any hesitation you feel is information about your hands rather than about the text. Type it the way you would type anything else. Do not slow down to be careful, and do not rush to beat last month. If a word comes out wrong, fix it the usual way and keep going. The numbers are only useful if the conditions stay the same: the same chair, the same keyboard, the same distance from the desk, and the same rules about looking. When something has changed, write it down beside the result. A result with an honest note is worth more than a clean result that hides a difference. Over a year, these monthly readings form a small table with one row per mode. Some rows will rise steadily. Others will stall for a while, or dip after a stretch of practice in another layout, and then recover. A missing row is not a zero; it is simply a month when that mode was not measured, and it stays visibly empty. Read the table slowly. It is not a scoreboard and it does not rank you against anyone. It is a record of how four different skills, living in the same pair of hands, are getting along with one another. When you reach the end of the passage, stop and rest your hands for a minute. Then look at the result, note anything unusual about today, and leave it alone until next month. The kettle will still be humming, the cat will still be on the radiator, and the jars will still be on the shelf, waiting for the next reading.

items.title: Numbers and symbols
items.text: The order arrived on 14 March: 36 jars at $2.75 each, 12 boxes at $9.40 each, and 1 crate of 250 labels (total: $220.80). The invoice listed item #4471 twice, so we called the office at 10:15 and asked them to check it. They agreed the second line was an error; the corrected total is $208.80, or about 5% less. Our notes say "paid in full on 2 April," with receipt no. 88-3016 filed under [A-F]. In the workshop, measurements follow a simple rule: cut once, measure twice, and write every number down. A shelf 1200 mm long needs 3 brackets spaced 450 mm apart; a 900 mm shelf needs only 2. The glue sets in 20-30 minutes at 18 C, but it needs 24 hours before any load over 15 kg. Keep the offcuts under 40 cm in the blue bin (not the red one!) and label each bin with its date: 03/09, 10/09, 17/09. A recipe for 4 people uses 500 g of flour, 350 ml of water, 10 g of salt, and 7 g of yeast. For 6 people multiply by 1.5: that is 750 g, 525 ml, 15 g, and 10.5 g. Bake at 230 degrees for 35-40 minutes; the loaf is done when its base sounds hollow. Score = (crust * 2 + crumb) / 3, rounded to 1 decimal place. Email the results to team@example.org with the subject "Batch 7 & 8 - results" and attach the table {date, weight, score}. Use the ~/notes/bakery folder, and back it up to /backup/2026 before Friday; 3 copies are better than 1. Is 7 x 8 = 56? Yes. Is 12 / 4 = 3? Also yes. Is 2 ^ 10 = 1024? Correct again! The path C:\data\reports\q3 holds last quarter's files, sorted by `size` and then by name; files matching *.tmp or *_old.* can be deleted after 30 days. Tickets cost 12 (adults), 6 (children) and 0 (under 3s); groups of 10+ get 15% off.

items.title: Javascript average
Python word count
Shell backup
items.text:
#!/bin/sh
# Copy today's notes into a dated backup folder.
set -eu
src="$HOME/notes"
dest="$HOME/backup/$(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
mkdir -p "$dest"
for f in "$src"/*.txt; do
  [ -e "$f" ] || continue
  cp -p "$f" "$dest/"
done
echo "copied $(ls "$dest" | wc -l) files to $dest"
